prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of flat electronic bands at magic twist angles in bilayer graphene and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene, founding moire quantum matter

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene offers the cleanest theory-to-experiment arc left on this list in my own field. Bistritzer and MacDonald's continuum model predicted, from the electronic structure of two rotated layers, that the Dirac-band velocity collapses and flat bands appear at a specific angle. Jarillo-Herrero's group then found correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle in 2018, and many independent groups have since reproduced the band-flattening picture. The resulting field is conceptually new: a single continuous knob, the twist angle, tunes bandwidth and interaction strength in a clean two-dimensional system, and it has produced Chern and fractional states. It also changed what electronic-structure theory is expected to do, since a Hamiltonian derived from the stacking geometry guided the experiment. I keep it first because of that originality and downstream influence, and because it avoids the overlap problems that burden other condensed-matter candidates (the 2016 topological-phase prize for B013, the 2025 circuits prize for B001).
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity and credit. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unsettled, device-to-device variability is real, and several colleagues (Lindroth, Kroll, Pearce, Johansson) judge recognition slightly early. The credit is also imperfect: Yuan Cao, the first author of the decisive experiments, and other moire pioneers cannot be named under the supplied credited names and the three-person cap, and the experimental credit rests on a group leader. By contrast B053 has far broader committee support, with six top-three placements, near-unanimous attribution to Katori and Ye, and strong multi-laboratory confirmation. If the committee puts maturity first, B053 is the safer and arguably more defensible choice, and I would not treat the gap as a scandal.

responses.point: Ranked optical lattice clocks first on clean attribution, 1e-18 uncertainties and global reproduction, and put twisted bilayer graphene last of her ballot as relatively young, with an unsettled superconducting mechanism and possible prematurity.
responses.response: I accept that B053 is more mature and that its two-name attribution is cleaner than anything in B033. But a precise, well-confirmed instrument lineage is a different standard from the one that has historically rewarded a new physical regime. I do not think the unresolved pairing mechanism undermines the core result: the flat-band prediction and the existence of correlated phases at the predicted angle are stable and independently reproduced across many groups for several years. Where I would concede ground is timing, and I would be comfortable if the committee ordered B053 ahead of B033 on that basis, but I do not agree that eight years of broad replication makes B033 premature. I also take her point about the 2005 comb prize, which is why I regard the metrology case as strong but not free of overlap.

responses.point: Placed circuit QED first, arguing it complements the 2025 prize without duplicating it, while ranking B013 second and B033 only fifth because the mechanism of superconductivity is still debated and the allocation between theory, first experiment and later groups is contested.
responses.response: I disagree on circuit QED. As chair of the 2025 cycle I would not say a second superconducting-circuit award is excluded, and I accept that cQED is distinct in content from macroscopic quantum tunnelling. But the 2025 prize has only just validated the platform, and an adjacent award a year later seems to me a poor use of the slot when other fields have waited longer. On B033 I share his concern about allocation, but I think the flat-band prediction and the first observation are separable enough for a clear theory-plus-experiment citation. I agree with him that B013 is among the strongest condensed-matter alternatives and that its credit problem, the missing Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposal, is the real obstacle to it.

responses.point: Ranked topological insulators first as a durable organising principle in the theory of matter and twisted bilayer graphene second, noting that the superconductivity and correlated phases are still debated and recognition may be somewhat early.
responses.response: I agree with him on the intellectual weight of B013 and I ranked it fourth only because of overlap with the 2016 prize and the credit problem. His ranking also shows the two condensed-matter candidates are not rivals so much as the same bet on theory-led discovery. Where I differ is that I would give B033 the edge because it has not been touched by an earlier prize and its three-name credit is cleaner than the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp-Hasan choice, which must leave out the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and one of Mele or Hasan. If the committee prefers the older field he proposes, I can support B013 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, but the 2016 overlap needs to be addressed directly in the citation.

responses.point: Ranked optical lattice clocks first because magic-wavelength trapping gives a concrete step in what can be measured, with independent agreement at the 1e-18 level, and placed twisted bilayer graphene sixth as probably slightly early.
responses.response: His case for B053 is the strongest on the table on confirmation and clarity, and I moved it to my first alternative. My remaining hesitation is not about merit but about the physics-versus-technology boundary: a clock is an extraordinary measurement tool, and its main payoff, a redefined second and tests of constants, is still prospective. I also share his concern that ion-clock work and the 2005 frequency-comb prize cover adjacent ground. I would ask him whether he would rank B053 above B033 even if the committee judged moire matter to be a genuinely new regime of correlated physics rather than a technique.

responses.point: Ranked aberration-corrected electron microscopy first as a decisive instrument-driven advance across materials physics, with clear measurable gain and timely or overdue recognition.
responses.response: As a theorist who uses the atomic-resolution data that corrected microscopes produce, I agree on its usefulness, and I ranked it seventh partly because I am not neutral about how much it benefits my field. My reservation is the physics-versus-method question she herself flags, and the credit gap around the STEM-corrector line (Krivanek, Dellby and Zach), which a Rose, Haider and Urban trio does not resolve. I am less persuaded that it should displace candidates that opened a new physical regime.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the missing experimental first author (Yuan Cao) and other moire pioneers as disqualifying for a three-name credit.
Whether the unsettled pairing mechanism makes B033 premature against B053, which has much broader opening support.
How much a close prior prize (2016 topological phases for B013, 2025 circuits for B001) should weigh against an otherwise strong candidate.
I rely on memory for dates, priority and roles and have not verified them.
statement.conflict_note: No specific personal or institutional connection to any shortlisted candidate or credited person is apparent from my profile. B033 and B013 are close to my own research area (electronic structure, magnetism and correlated electrons), and B052 supplies data used by materials theory, so I note a possible field bias in favour of condensed-matter theory. I also served as chair for the 2025 cycle, which may colour my view of B001 given the closely related 2025 award.
